According to the results, published on Thursday (November 19), WMG generated total revenues of USD $2.001 billion in the quarter.

This is the first time WMG ‘s quarterly revenues have crossed the $2 billion mark, beating the company’s previous record of $1.868 billion, set in calendar Q3 2025.

Other highlights from the quarter include recorded music revenues up 7.3% YoY at constant currency to $1.639 billion.

Within that figure, recorded music subscription streaming revenues were up 14.7% YoY at constant currency to $804 million.

Artist services and expanded-rights revenue, meanwhile, fell 19.9% YoY at constant currency to $257 million, which WMG linked to higher merchandising revenue in the prior-year quarter from its Oasis partnership.

items.headline: Chris Campbell, bassist of Bob Seger's Silver Bullet Band, dies at 78
items.summary: Rolling Stone reported that he died on Sunday of natural causes, according to his widow. He joined Seger in 1969 and played with him for about 50 years, until the 2019 farewell tour ended.
items.matters: he was on the band's breakthrough 1976 albums "Live Bullet" and "Night Moves".
items.body:
Chris Campbell, longtime bassist for Bob Seger's Silver Bullet Band, has passed away. Rolling Stone reports that Campbell died on Sunday and that his widow Courtney says he died of natural causes. Campbell was 78.

Chris Campbell grew up in Plymouth, Michigan, outside Detroit. He joined forces with Bob Seger in 1969 and then played with him for 50 years, until Seger's retirement tour in 2019. Seger and his band, the Bob Seger System, had just released their first national hit, "Ramblin' Gamblin' Man," one year earlier, after original bassist Dan Honaker broke his wrist in a motorcycle accident. When Seger started the Silver Bullet Band, his next group, he offered Campbell the bassist spot.

Seger was mostly a Midwestern sensation in the mid-'70s, but he and his band broke out nationally with the hugely successful 1976 albums Live Bullet and Night Moves. They kept up a relentless touring pace for decades, though they did take a 10-year break in the '90s and '00s. Campbell, along with saxophonist Alto Reed and backup singers Shaun Murphy and Laura Creamer, stayed with the band all the way up until Seger's retirement tour ended with a 2019 show in Philadelphia. After the tour ended Campbell sued Seger and manager Punch Andrews for unpaid royalties. Campbell lost the lawsuit.

items.headline: FTC and seven states ask a court to strike 10 of Live Nation and Ticketmaster's 12 defences in the BOTS Act case
items.summary: the 19 November filing in Los Angeles targets defences that blame scalpers, claim the law is too vague, or invoke waiver and estoppel.
items.matters: the FTC alleges consumers paid over $16.4bn in Ticketmaster fees from 2019 to 2024. A hearing is set for 7 January 2027, and a separate antitrust verdict against the companies from April still awaits a ruling on their challenge.
items.body:
The US Federal Trade Commission and seven states have asked a federal judge to throw out 10 of the 12 defenses that Live Nation and Ticketmaster have raised against their ticket-resale lawsuit.

Among them is the companies’ argument that the actions of scalpers and bot operators, rather than Ticketmaster ‘s own conduct, caused any harm to fans.

The motion was filed in federal court in Los Angeles on Thursday (November 19). The filing, obtained by MBW, can be read in full here.

The lawsuit, filed in September 2025, alleges that Ticketmaster knowingly let brokers spread their purchases across multiple accounts to get around the ticket limits set by artists.

According to the complaint, this let Ticketmaster “triple dip” on fees, charging brokers when they bought the tickets, charging them again when the tickets were relisted on its own resale marketplace, and charging the fans who bought them there.

The plaintiffs say this breaches the Better Online Ticket Sales (BOTS) Act, a 2016 law that, among other things, bars selling tickets the seller knew, or should have known, were bought by getting around the systems used to enforce purchase limits.

The suit also alleges that the prices Ticketmaster first showed fans did not include mandatory fees that were added at checkout.

The FTC and the states want civil penalties and other monetary relief, plus a court order stopping the practices described in the complaint.

No damages or penalty figure is given in the complaint, which states that consumers paid more than USD $16.4 billion in mandatory fees on Ticketmaster purchases from 2019 through 2024.

It says Ticketmaster charged USD $3.7 billion in fees on resale tickets in those years.

“If not stricken, Defendants’ affirmative defenses will prolong the litigation, lead to wasteful discovery, and unnecessarily consume the parties’ and the Court’s resources,” the FTC and the states argue.

The motion notes that an affirmative defense is meant to defeat a claim even if every element of it is proven.

It argues that several of the companies’ defenses instead simply deny the allegations, which Live Nation and Ticketmaster have already done elsewhere in their answer.

The FTC and the states want most of the defenses struck permanently, with no chance to rewrite them, because the companies have already amended their answer once.

items.headline: Worth watching this week: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, in IMAX from today
items.summary: the Tarantino-written, Fincher-directed sequel is set in Los Angeles in summer 1977 and stars Brad Pitt, with Elizabeth Debicki.
items.matters: reviews are split: TheWrap calls it "just okay" and says Fincher's direction is stylish but the plot thin, while the search results show Variety calling it very fun and The A.V. Club calling it a misfire. It reaches Netflix on 23 December.
items.body:
As a director, Tarantino loves those empty spaces. He proved he can shoot all-timer action sequences in “Kill Bill” and “Death Proof,” but that didn’t stop him from letting his characters shoot their mouths off for pages anyway. By the time he got to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” it seemed like he finally dropped all the pretense and made his ultimate hangout movie. An actor and a stuntman, drifting from one industry anecdote to another, until they finally murdered the Manson Family as an afterthought. Nevermind what it meant. It was just something Tarantino wanted to do, a fantasy to live out surreptitiously, much like his script for “True Romance,” where a kung fu film fan proves to be such a virile and macho ladies man that even Elvis Presley’s ghost looks up to him.

The sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has all of Tarantino’s voluminous speeches and narrative sidetracks, but this time it’s directed by David Fincher, whose films are stylish but infinitely more focused. It’s refreshing to see what someone else can do with Tarantino’s screenplays again. Fincher films dialogue as a means of narrative propulsion, so “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has a breakneck pace even though, for most of the movie, not much actually happens.

“Cliff Booth” stars Brad Pitt, reprising his role as a charismatic, laid back stuntman who also loves killing. He killed his wife with a harpoon gun and got away with it, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” left slightly ambiguous but Tarantino confirmed in the novelization. Some people had a hard time believing that Booth was a wife-murderer, because he seems so nice, but that’s officially who he is. He’s effortlessly charming and then kills a person and feels nothing, and for some reason that’s not supposed to detract from his likability. It’s a, let’s say, “interesting” stance to take in an industry where alleged abusers are given countless opportunities to redeem their careers while victims are forced into the background.

A lot of people loved Cliff Booth in his first feature film appearance. Some of us didn’t, but it’s easier to root for him in his “Further Mis-Adventures,” where he’s a self-appointed avenging angel of Hollywood’s favorite, arguably less morally compromised celebs.

Set in the summer of 1977, the film finds Booth zooming across Los Angeles from one gig to another, slinging margaritas at Tiki Bars, running a film projector at The New Beverly (which Tarantino now owns), and barrel-rolling at demolition derbies. But his most interesting side hustle is solving illegal problems for…

items.headline: Netflix renews French action thriller "Elite Force" for season 2
items.summary: filming began in the Paris region on 23 November and is scheduled to run through at least mid-April 2027, with Julien Leclercq directing and Tomer Sisley returning.
items.matters: season 1 launched on 22 July, topped Netflix's global non-English TV chart for two weeks and drew about 20.9 million views in four weeks.
items.body:
Production is now underway in Paris for the second season of Julien Leclercq's global hit action thriller Elite Force.

After debuting at number one on Netflix’s global non-English chart last July, French action thriller Elite Force is heading back for a sophomore season, with cameras now rolling in Paris. Here’s everything we know so far about season 2 of Elite Force.

Co-created by Julien Leclercq and Sylvain Caron, the six-part series (known as GIGN in France) landed on Netflix on July 22nd, 2026, and looked like a likely candidate for renewal from the off. Even so, Netflix held back any news on its scripted shows at its October upfronts.

The hints have been there, though. Shortly after release, Tomer Sisley said a second season was already being written, and he later told Télé Loisirs that the show’s producer had scheduled a meeting last August. The official renewal comes after Julien Leclercq shared a season 2 script on November 13th on social media:

In short: very well for a French-language series. Elite Force spent four weeks in Netflix’s global non-English TV top 10, including two weeks at number one, picking up 20.9 million views and 103 million hours viewed along the way.

That opening week is worth a second look, too. With a Wednesday release, the show had just five days to rack up its 10.1 million views.

The reach was just as impressive. According to our top 10 data, Elite Force featured in the weekly TV top 10s of 91 countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Germany, Spain, Italy, India and Mexico.

Unsurprisingly, it had the longest legs closer to home. The show charted for five weeks in France, Switzerland, Ukraine and New Caledonia, and for four weeks in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Morocco, Lebanon and Nigeria. Most of the rest of Europe kept it around for three weeks, while the majority of the Americas and Asia-Pacific saw it drop out after two.

The drop-off after week two was steep, but a number one debut and a 91-country footprint is a rare result for a French Netflix Original, particularly at a time when few of them (Blood Coast aside) have been handed more episodes.

Filming is already underway. According to casting calls posted on Figurants.com, cameras began rolling in the Paris region on Monday, November 23rd, with shoot dates scheduled through to at least mid-April 2027.

items.matters: BBC Studios has a separate deal to take the CBeebies brand to Netflix outside the UK (excluding China), with no dates yet, and the shows stay on iPlayer.
items.body:
A landmark partnership will see a dedicated CBeebies hub launch on Netflix UK this December before rolling out globally.

Netflix’s kids library is about to get a lot more British. The BBC and Netflix have announced a new partnership that will see a dedicated CBeebies hub launch on Netflix in the UK on December 2, with a global rollout also in the works and Netflix putting money into brand-new CBeebies shows.

Both companies are describing this as a limited trial. The BBC says it wants to test whether putting a sample of its preschool lineup on Netflix can extend CBeebies’ reach and visibility, and whether that viewing can be attributed back to the BBC.

Importantly, nothing is leaving the BBC’s own platforms. Every show in the trial stays on BBC iPlayer, which remains the home of the full CBeebies lineup alongside the linear channel and YouTube. The BBC stresses that the Netflix selection is only a small part of the wider CBeebies offering.

Netflix is no stranger to British preschool favorites, of course, with the likes of Shaun the Sheep and Hey Duggee already streaming. What’s different here is the branding: rather than individual licensed titles scattered across the kids catalog, CBeebies gets its own space.

The deal isn’t limited to the UK. BBC Studios has brokered a separate distribution deal that will bring the CBeebies brand experience to Netflix members outside the UK, with additional titles in the mix. No dates or title lists have been confirmed for international regions just yet.

There are some exceptions. The global deal does not include China, and the BBC notes that BBC Studios already has exclusive partnerships in place in New Zealand and South Africa.

Perhaps the most significant detail for the UK kids TV industry is that Netflix has committed to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions as part of the partnership.

Netflix has spent the past year working hard to win over parents, and CBeebies is about as trusted as preschool brands get, especially in the UK and hopefully soon, globally. Filmed over the course of a year, the documentary uses Elba’s own story as its way in. Growing up in Hackney, he received a grant from what was then The Prince’s Trust, which helped launch his acting career. Alongside Elba looking back, the documentary follows three young people chasing their ambitions with the Trust’s support today and the hurdles they’re up against.

items.summary: the Digital Omnibus on AI added prohibitions on AI that generates non-consensual intimate imagery of identifiable people and on AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
items.matters: providers of general-purpose image and video generators must show adequate safeguards such as refusal training, output controls and content filtering, since terms of use alone won't be enough, and fines go up to €35m or 7% of turnover.
items.body:
Since 2 February 2025, eight categories of AI practices have been banned in the EU because they pose unacceptable risks to fundamental rights and Union values. These ‘prohibited practices’ are set out in Article 5 of the AI Act. In 2026, the Digital Omnibus added two further prohibitions, which apply from 2 December 2026. Breaching these prohibitions can attract the highest fines available under the AI Act: up to €35 million or 7% of an undertaking’s total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

The European Commission’s Guidelines on prohibited AI practices explain how the Commission interprets the original eight prohibitions, set out the conditions that must be met for each to apply, and give examples of practices the Commission considers to fall inside or outside their scope. The Guidelines are not legally binding, and authoritative interpretation of the AI Act rests with the Court of Justice of the EU. Even so, they are the clearest indication of how the Commission expects Article 5 to work in practice.

This post summarises what the Guidelines say about the eight original prohibitions, and separately explains the two prohibitions added in 2026.

Before turning to the individual bans, the Guidelines clarify three important points about their scope.

First, Article 5 can apply to both providers of AI systems and their deployers. Their responsibilities are different: providers are responsible for the systems they place on the market or put into service, while deployers are responsible for how they use them.

Finally, an AI system that falls outside an Article 5 prohibition is not necessarily unregulated. It may still be classified as high-risk, and other EU rules, including data protection and consumer law, may continue to apply.

Our goal is to build the most useful, authoritative, and comprehensive guide to the AI Act anywhere on the internet. We’ll never put this behind a paywall or use it to sell you a service. We do this because we think good AI governance matters, and that means making authoritative guidance genuinely accessible.

This website is built and maintained by the Future of Life Institute — the world’s oldest and largest nonprofit working for the responsible development of AI.

Each prohibition has its own conditions and, in some cases, exceptions. A practice falls within a particular prohibition only where its relevant conditions are met. Below are the clarifications which may be most relevant in practice.

items.matters: it follows a May 2026 non-compliance decision and a €200m fine. It shows what regulators expect from a risk assessment, including measurable mitigation and a check on whether your own recommender amplifies illegal listings.
items.body:
The European Commission has accepted Temu's action plan to comply with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and tackle the availability of illegal products online.

The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content.

The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings.

The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan.

The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026, in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine.

items.body:
Isack Hadjar has received a 10-second penalty for driving unnecessarily slowly in Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix – the result of his actions under the safety car.

The race was neutralised on lap 19 when Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara collided; Max Verstappen was leading team-mate Hadjar but the Red Bulls and Mercedes cars lay within just over a second; the double-stack meant Hadjar risked losing track position to Russell and other drivers.

The Frenchman therefore slowed down, to the extent that he was 4.288s slower than his team-mate on that lap. This mitigated the effect of the double-stack, though he still couldn’t retain second position.

Hadjar has now landed a 10-second penalty, whose impact actually is marginal, dropping him from 14th to 15th after his front wing broke at the restart.

“While driving on the straight between Turns 13 and 14 under Safety Car conditions, the driver of Car 6 received repeated instructions from his team stating ‘five seconds, five seconds, five seconds’,” the stewards’ report read.

“Following these instructions, Car 6 significantly reduced its speed, at one point travelling approximately 100km/h slower than Car 3, which was ahead of it. The Stewards determined that this significant reduction in speed was deliberate and intended to create a gap to the car ahead and was not made for safety reasons, thereby allowing the team to perform a double-stack pitstop without Car 6 losing time waiting behind its team-mate in the pitlane.

“Furthermore, this manoeuvre directly impacted the cars following Car 6, which were forced to reduce their speed accordingly and could not overtake Car 6 due to the restrictions applicable under Safety Car conditions.

The aforementioned clash, with Perez spinning Camara around and breaking his Cadillac’s suspension, earned the Mexican a five-place grid penalty for the Qatar round.

“Car 11 (PER) attempted to overtake Car 51 (CAM) on the inside, on the left-hand side, approaching Turn 14,” the stewards wrote.

“The Stewards noted that at no point during the manoeuvre was the front axle of Car 11 at least alongside the mirror of Car 51. The two cars collided at the entry to Turn 14, resulting in Car 11 retiring from the Race.

items.body:
The post-race media session with Ferrari Formula 1 team boss Frederic Vasseur in Las Vegas was, in several respects, almost a carbon copy of the conversation in Mexico City.

On both occasions, the discussion with the written press took place in a small, almost cosy room at the back of the Ferrari hospitality area, partly because Formula 1 teams cannot rely on the hospitality units used during the European part of the season when travelling to flyaway races.

Just as in Mexico, there was considerable media interest, and just as at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, one topic dominated the conversation: the clash between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

Before Vasseur arrived, as the press officer tried to create a little more space, a colleague remarked that the room had quite a relaxing atmosphere. The press officer laughed: "Well, it's a very relaxing evening for us as well…"

It was, of course, sarcastic. This time, the collision between the two red cars had not cost Ferrari a potential 1-2 finish, unlike in Mexico, but that did nothing to ease Vasseur's frustration.

"Honestly, you can't imagine the frustration for me, but it’s even more important for all the guys at home," the Ferrari team principal said.

Apart from the word 'frustration', another word that came up during the session was 'powerless'. Following the clash in Mexico, constructive discussions were held in Sao Paulo, with all parties subsequently saying that those talks had been very productive and that the limits had been established.

The central message was that a driver's interests must never take precedence over those of 2,000 team members back in Maranello, and that the drivers must never let those team members and sponsors down through actions that harm the team.

When Autosport asked whether, in a sense, Vasseur felt powerless, given that he had clearly communicated that message but it had still proved insufficient once the visors came down, the Ferrari team principal responded: "That is a good point… And that's why I want to once again have a discussion tomorrow, also to try to digest the situation.

"I think it's not the right place to discuss it with them two minutes after the race. I saw Charles a bit down and I told him what I have to say. I've got to discuss the rest with him tomorrow."

items.headline: Bearman is the only driver still without a 2027 contract
items.summary: his expected Haas deal remains unsigned, while nearly every other 2027 seat is confirmed and Haas is the only team changing its line-up.
items.matters: it is the last open seat on the 2027 grid, and Cadillac kept Valtteri Bottas rather than promoting Colton Herta.
items.body:
Ferrari protege Oliver Bearman remains the only driver on the F1 grid without a contract for 2027. It is a situation that would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago, given that his retention at Haas had been taken for granted since last summer.

The announcement of Rafael Camara as Bearman's 2027 team-mate, which came ahead of the Brazilian Grand Prix, was expected to be swiftly followed by that of his British team-mate. Instead, the silence has dragged on to the point of becoming a talking point, even prompting rumours of Bearman driving elsewhere next year. The paradox is that Bearman and Haas have strong reasons to reach an agreement.

Bearman has ruled out racing elsewhere in 2027, while Haas has long been expected to retain him, yet the negotiations have dragged on far longer than initially anticipated.

In recent weeks, there has been speculation about the reasons for the deadlock, some linked to the contractual relationship between Bearman and Ferrari and to the future prospects of the 21-year-old Briton.

Ferrari has already exercised the option allowing it to retain Bearman within its driver programme. Given that Maranello has invested financial resources in the young Briton ever since he joined the Driver Academy in 2021, allowing Bearman to leave on a free transfer would be a big waste of all those efforts.

Rafael Camara will finish the 2026 season for Haas as he prepares for his full 2027 debut alongside Oliver Bearman.

Bearman could be in a position to leave Ferrari at the end of 2027 if he has not received a call-up to join the works team, but this scenario does not represent an obstacle to renewing with Haas, and there is no need to finalise his relationship with Ferrari in the short term – especially given that Lewis Hamilton is in the twilight of his career. The Scuderia has not ruled out any of its longer-term options.

The immediate negotiations therefore centre on two parties: Haas and Bearman’s entourage. The sticking point is the salary offered by the American team, a figure that the driver and his staff do not consider commensurate with their expectations.

The Briton admitted that the uncertainty is becoming difficult to cope with, especially after a season in which he believes he has proved his worth as the team's lead driver. Bearman categorically ruled out the possibility of moving to another team in 2027, though. items.headline: Aeon on how horses, not grain, built the first states
items.summary: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene's essay (16 November, about 8,100 words) argues that states grew out of mobility and animal transport rather than grain farming. He says the grain-first theory was shaped by Cold War politics and writes pastoralist conquest out of the story.
items.body:
Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga…
